prompt: By the lesson's definition, what is business intelligence?
hint: Work, not a product; records, answers, decisions.

choices.text: A category of software for drawing charts from a database
choices.why: That describes the tools. The lesson says a company can own them all and have no BI.

choices.text: Turning the records a company keeps into answers to its decisions, the same way each time
choices.why: Right: records, answers to decisions, and repeatability are the three parts of the definition.

choices.text: Collecting new data through surveys and interviews so that the company finally knows who its customers are
choices.why: BI starts from records the company already keeps to run itself, not from surveys.

choices.text: Predicting the future with statistical models
choices.why: Prediction is one kind of analysis (lesson 8) and model building is mostly a data scientist's job.

prompt: Two directors brought different totals for the same week to Varanda's Monday meeting. What does the lesson say was the cause?
hint: Neither of them was wrong.

choices.text: One of them had copied the file from the stores' system incorrectly
choices.why: The lesson says neither was wrong; a copying error would have made one of them wrong.

choices.text: The online shop sent its file late
choices.why: Lateness explains a missing number, not two different ones arrived at by two people on time.

choices.text: Two unwritten definitions of when an online sale counts
choices.why: Right: one counted orders on the day placed, the other on the day paid, and neither definition was written down.

choices.text: The spreadsheet rounded each store's total differently
choices.why: Rounding moves a total by a little and the same way for everybody; it does not give two directors two answers.

prompt: A number becomes an answer when it carries a definition, a period and a ___, because without it nobody can tell whether the result was good.
Why does the lesson call BI's reliance on existing records both a strength and a weakness?
hint: The receipt and the barbecue.

choices.text: They are cheap to store, but they take far too long to load into any BI tool to be useful
choices.why: Storage and loading time are not the lesson's point; what the records leave out is.

choices.text: They are accurate, but the tax authority may see them
choices.why: The tax authority is one reason the records exist, and it has nothing to do with what they can answer.

choices.text: They are recent, but they hold no history
choices.why: Records accumulate history; the lesson's comparison with 2024 depends on it.

choices.text: They are complete and already paid for, but they record what happened and not why
choices.why: Right: the receipt records the hose and not the barbecue the customer could not find.

prompt: Match each situation to the wrong picture of BI it shows.
hint: Tool, dashboard, report factory, the truth by default.

pairs.left: A company buys licences for three BI products and nobody can say what the sales figure means
Two hundred reports exist and nobody knows which are read
A total includes online orders counted twice, and nothing on the screen says so
pairs.right: BI as the truth by default

pairs.left: A store manager hunting today's late orders is given a chart of the last twelve months

prompt: Helena reads the Monday sales figure on her phone before the meeting. What form does the lesson say it takes?
hint: The question decides the form.

choices.text: Two lines in an email
choices.why: Right: the form follows how and when she reads it, and a dashboard would add nothing.

choices.text: A dashboard with a chart for each store
choices.why: That is the picture the lesson corrects: a dashboard is one way of delivering an answer, not the default.

choices.text: A printed report placed on the meeting table
choices.why: She reads it before the meeting, on her phone; paper on the table arrives too late for that.

choices.text: A spreadsheet she filters herself
choices.why: Handing the CEO the raw sheet moves the analyst's work to her and gives her nothing to read on a phone.

prompt: According to the lesson, what separates an analyst doing BI from one running a print shop?
hint: One question, asked before building.

choices.text: The number of reports delivered each month
choices.why: A count of reports is exactly what a print shop maximises; the lesson says it is invisible to the real failure.

choices.text: Whether the reports are built in a BI tool or in a spreadsheet
choices.why: The tool is not what BI is; a disciplined analyst with a spreadsheet does BI.

choices.text: Asking "what will you decide with this?" before building anything
choices.why: Right: the question ties the work to a decision, and lesson 4 turns it into a routine.

choices.text: Refusing every request that has not come from a director
choices.why: Rank is not the test. A store manager's request tied to a decision is worth more than a director's curiosity.

prompt: Varanda considers a chatbot that answers "what were sales last week?" in plain language. By the lesson, what does it still need?
hint: The two directors and their two totals.

choices.text: A dashboard behind it, so the answers can be checked visually
choices.why: A picture of the same undefined number does not settle which number is right.

choices.text: A written definition of a sale behind it
choices.why: Right: without it, the chatbot gives two people two totals, just more confidently.

choices.text: A data scientist to retrain it every week
choices.why: Retraining changes how it talks, not what a sale is.

choices.text: Nothing more: a chatbot is a complete BI system
choices.why: The lesson calls it a new way of asking, with the same need for a definition as any spreadsheet.

prompt: Put the steps of the BI cycle in order, starting where a lap starts.
hint: It starts with somebody who has to decide something.
trap: Starting with the data is the most common way the cycle is broken, which is why it is the tempting first step.

prompt: An analysis shows that Varanda sells more umbrellas when it rains. Which failure of the cycle does the lesson use this to illustrate?
hint: True and useless.

choices.text: Stopping at the answer: the finding was shown and nobody acted
choices.why: That failure is the dashboard visited only by its author. The umbrella finding fails earlier.

choices.text: Bad data: the weather records were incomplete
choices.why: Nothing says the data was wrong; the finding is true.

choices.text: Starting from the data instead of from a question
choices.why: Right: with no decision behind it, the analysis produced something true that nobody needed.

choices.text: Choosing the method before understanding the question
choices.why: That is a failure of the analysis step; here there was no question to understand in the first place.

prompt: A year after Helena's chosen store is enlarged, its sales are 12% higher. Why does the lesson's cycle say to compare it with the stores that were not touched as well?
hint: What else could have raised sales that year?

choices.text: Because the untouched stores are the next ones to be enlarged
choices.why: Perhaps, but that is a different decision; the comparison is about whether this one worked.

choices.text: Because sales rose across the company too, and the works deserve credit only for the difference
choices.why: Right: the company grew 5.7% in 2025 untouched; measuring against what would have happened anyway is the point.

choices.text: Because a store's own history is unreliable after building work
choices.why: The store's history is fine; on its own it just cannot separate the works from everything else.

choices.text: Because the board asks for every store in the same report
choices.why: Report format has nothing to do with measuring what a decision did.

prompt: Which of these does the lesson name as ways the BI cycle goes wrong? Choose all that apply.
hint: One per step of the table.

choices.text: The data that is easy to get stands in for the data that matters
choices.why: Right: the failure of the data step.

choices.text: Everything is shown, so nothing is
choices.why: Right: the failure of the presentation step.

choices.text: The analysis uses a spreadsheet instead of a BI tool
choices.why: The lesson never counts the tool as a failure; a spreadsheet is what this course uses.

choices.text: Nobody is named to own the decision
choices.why: Right: the failure of the decision step — nothing is decided.

choices.text: The question comes from a director rather than from the analyst
choices.why: Questions should come from the people who decide; that is how the cycle is meant to start.

prompt: In your sheet, what share of Varanda's 2025 sales did the online shop make, in percent rounded to one decimal?
You copy C2, written as =ROUND(B2/B12*100,1) with no $, down to C3. What goes wrong?
hint: Which cells does the copy in C3 point at?

choices.text: C3 shows the same share as C2
choices.why: Both references move when copied, so C3 points at B3, not B2.

choices.text: C3 divides by B13, which is empty
choices.why: Right: the total's reference moves down too, and dividing by an empty cell gives #DIV/0!.

choices.text: The shares stop adding up to 99.9 and add up to exactly 100
choices.why: Nothing about the $ changes the rounding; the copy breaks the formula instead.

choices.text: The spreadsheet refuses to copy a formula that has no $ in it
choices.why: Spreadsheets copy any formula; the problem is what the copy points at.

prompt: The ten shares in your sheet add up to 99.9. What does the lesson say a report should do about it?
hint: Each share was rounded on its own.

choices.text: Add the missing 0.1 to the largest share so the column says 100
choices.why: That is the nudge the lesson calls dishonest: it makes one share say something untrue.

choices.text: Recompute the shares with more decimals until the sum reaches 100
choices.why: More decimals shrink the gap and change nothing about why it exists; the lesson keeps one decimal.

choices.text: Show them as they are: rounded shares adding to 99.9 are honest
choices.why: Right: the gap comes from rounding each share separately, and hiding it would be the mistake.

choices.text: Drop the online shop from the column
choices.why: Removing a line changes the question, and the online shop is the largest one.

prompt: In the three-store copy, Pampulha's 10560 arrives as text. What does =SUM(B2:B4) return?
hint: SUM skips text without saying so.

prompt: Match what the spreadsheet shows to the mistake behind it.
hint: Two are errors, two are quiet.

pairs.right: A function name from another language
A reference pointing at an empty cell

pairs.left: A total R$ 10.56 million short, with no error

pairs.right: A thousands separator read as a decimal point

prompt: Why does the lesson treat the text number and the thousands separator as worse than #NAME? and #DIV/0!?
hint: Which ones reach a meeting?

choices.text: They give a plausible number and no error, so nobody looks
choices.why: Right: an error stops you; a quiet wrong total is the one that gets presented.

choices.text: They happen more often than error codes in every spreadsheet product
choices.why: The lesson makes no claim about frequency; it is about what you can see.

choices.text: They cannot be fixed once the file has been saved
choices.why: Both are fixed by retyping the number; the danger is not noticing.

choices.text: They only happen in LibreOffice
choices.why: SUM skips text and separators follow the locale in all three spreadsheets the lesson names.

prompt: Before trusting a pasted column, the habit that catches all five mistakes is to check one ___ by hand against the original.
hint: A single line of the table.

prompt: A director asks Lívia for "a dashboard with all our data on it". What should she do first, by this lesson?
hint: Where does a lap of the cycle begin?

choices.text: Choose a BI tool and connect it to every system
choices.why: That starts from the tool and the data, the two places the lesson says a lap must not start.

choices.text: Build a first version quickly so he has something to react to
choices.why: A quick version of the wrong thing is still the wrong thing; there is no decision yet to build for.

choices.text: Ask which decisions he will make with it
choices.why: Right: the question comes first, and "all our data" is the sign it is missing.

choices.text: List every report Varanda already has and merge them
choices.why: Merging two hundred unread reports is the report factory at a larger scale.

prompt: Which of these would the lesson count as business intelligence at Varanda? Choose all that apply.
hint: Records, an answer to a decision, the same way every time.

choices.text: One written definition of a sale, computed in one place, sent before nine every Monday
choices.why: Right: that was BI's first job at Varanda.

choices.text: A licence for a BI product that nobody has opened yet
choices.why: A tool with no answers in it is not BI.

choices.text: A monthly email with each store's share of sales, defined and compared with last year
choices.why: Right: a small, defined, repeated answer — no dashboard needed.

choices.text: A one-off survey asking customers what they think of the stores
choices.why: Useful research, but it is new data collected once, not the company's records answered repeatedly.

prompt: Lívia's new total for Monday differs from the one Otávio used to type by hand. Which response fits this lesson best?
hint: Neither of the old totals was wrong either.

choices.text: Adjust the new pipeline until it matches the old number, which people trust
choices.why: Matching an unwritten definition by trial and error keeps the problem and hides it.

choices.text: Publish the new number and stop explaining, since it comes from a system
choices.why: A number from a system is not the truth by default; the difference needs an explanation.

choices.text: Find which definition each uses, write the chosen one down and show the difference
choices.why: Right: the difference is almost certainly two definitions, and writing one down is the job.

choices.text: Send both numbers every week and let each director choose
choices.why: That makes the two-totals meeting permanent.
